title: Olanzapine
subtitle: The frontier guide to psychiatric medications
text:
This newsletter’s author is a psychiatrist, who is saying goodbye to “medication management” as part of his practice. As part of this decision, Owen is writing a series of articles summarizing what he learned about psychiatric medications as he makes the decision to see what happens when he focuses his efforts entirely on biological but non-once daily oral medication treatments. Neuromodulation is the future of the field…and in my day today practice, I focus on that new modality of neuromodulation

On the other hand, I spent years learning to manage oral medicines. So this article is about the trade offs in a sometimes life saving oral treatment.

A farewell to meds, as it were…

Share The Frontier Psychiatrists

Olanzapine is the second “atypical antipsychotic” medication brought market after clozapine—Risperidone was the first. It was introduced in 1996. Antipsychotic medications are divided into before and after. An earlier generation of medications, starting with Thorazine, robustly blocked certain dopamine receptors in the brain— D2 receptors. The mechanistic role of D2 receptors has recently been called into question.

Dopamine. It's weird. It is the most popular of neurotransmitters in popular parlance. This is because of its role in the reward center of the brain, an area called the nucleus accumbens. Reward gets a lot of press. The crucial role of dopamine in the ventral striatum, attention, and movement is less flashy.

What is olanzapine (Zyprexa)?

Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic, and that means close to nothing. It blocks dopamine D2 receptors, and many other sites. As we've recently learned, this is far from the whole story when it comes to how these drugs act.

Our author believes that a lot of the receptor profile stuff that Psychiatrists obsess about is much ado about not much. I’m a brain circuit maxi, and only slightly interested in any individual receptor this or that. I think that's the way to sell the feeling of being an expert, brought to you by pharma.

The key things to understand about olanzapine are:

It is very tolerable in the short term.

Olanzapine has the same anticholinergic load as including 300 mg of Benadryl with a traditional antipsychotic like haloperidol. This means there's a low risk of acute dystonic reactions—the anticholinergic effects balances out the dopamine blocking affect via its activity on gaba-ergic interneurons.

It is very sedating in the short term.

You can give a lot of olanzapine, up to 30mg, all at once, to someone who's never gotten the medication before, and they will be sedated. They will likely fall asleep. They will likely stay asleep for most of the next 30 hours, which is the half-life of the medicine.

This is not great if you're walking around and going out to coffee, but it's not bad if you're treating someone who's acutely agitated and might hurt themselves or somebody else. A lot of people who come in to a psychiatric hospital haven't slept very well, and so it may be that the sedation leading to additional sleep is part of the thing that makes this such a useful medication. If the reason you're agitated in the first place is because of mania—and mania is made worse by reduce sleep—then sedation is a feature, not a bug.

It is available as a tablet, as a rapid acting injectable, as a dissolvable tablet, and as a long acting injectable antipsychotic.

You can get a olanzapine in almost any formulation. There is not a patch, but other than that, it comes in the format that you would need as a physician.

Long acting injectable (LAI) olanzapine has a very specific and highly regulated risk profile: post injection delirium sedation syndrome. This is a rather unpleasant side effect that requires three hours of monitoring with an EKG in a clinic setting every month, at every dose of this monthly long acting injectable medicine.

This was always a problem, and never going to be something that got to market at scale. I am shocked they bothered to roll out this medicine in its LAI format, but they did, so I have to tell you about it. There is some sense that individuals who have died as a side effect of an injection with Zyprexa Relprevv, which is the brand name of this drug, died because the drug was accidentally injected into a vein or artery and not into a muscle. Regardless, it's not a drug to be administered without appropriate supervision.

It causes massive weight gain in almost everybody.

Olanzapine is a horrific drug when it comes to weight gain, dyslipidemia, and metabolic syndrome. Its only competitor in this regard is clozapine. I am generally of the opinion that if it's worth taking olanzapine opinion it's worth taking clozapine.

The risk profile is close to identical when it comes to the very serious and highly likely side effects of metabolic syndrome. Clozapine had additional risk from neutropenia, or other rare complications, and requires additional monitoring. I consider this to be a benefit to people who need a medicine this serious.

It is a pain in the neck to get additional monitoring, but it also forces doctors to do additional monitoring… and thus create a rhythm of regular check ins. That can be a good thing if you have schizophrenia or severe bipolar disorder.

Olanzapine does not require that kind of close monitoring for a specific adverse effect like agranulocytosis and neutropenia1, and therefore I don't think it's as good. This has little to do with the drug and everything to do with the behavior of humans who build trust with each other when they have to check in regularly about something quotidian.

Olanzapine causes gain weight in a way that's eventually catastrophic for many, but doesn't force you to check in with your doctor regularly for bloodwork, and that means more unchecked side effects and less relationship building. It's those relationships that are really helpful over time.

Olanzapine is a remarkably effective drug in the short term, but a for many can be a catastrophic drug to stay on over the long term if you don't need it. Like all things, there is a risk and benefit ratio to be mindful of, and it both can help one disease, but cause others. We take obesity too lightly historically, and I think that is a problem.
